title: Caught in 4K: The Aurora Files

reading.body:
This incident shows an AI coding and automation tool being used as an active component in a ransomware attack chain. Cursor Agent, which runs on Claude Sonnet, was directed by human operators to carry out network reconnaissance and exploitation tasks, including network scanning, domain enumeration, and NTLM relay attacks, against multiple organizations. The operators set explicit constraints on what the agent could do, prohibiting DCSync attacks, account lockouts, and adding computer objects to domains, which shows deliberate human direction of the AI's actions rather than autonomous operation.

The failure mode here is not a model malfunction. The tool functioned as designed, executing the tasks it was given. The problem is that a general-purpose AI agent capable of running network operations was accessible to actors who used it for criminal exploitation. No check within the tool is reported to have detected or blocked the malicious use pattern, and it is not established that any such safeguard was in place or attempted.

What is not established is who specifically controls the Aurora ransomware operation, whether any legal action has been taken against them, and whether Cursor or Anthropic had any knowledge of or means to detect this misuse at the time it occurred.

reports.title: Russian-speaking cybercriminals used SpaceX’s Cursor AI tool to hack seven companies
Aurora ransomware targets ESXi, abuses Cursor Agent for exploitation

summary:
# Summary

Gambit Security's Threat Intelligence team discovered that Aurora ransomware, active since April 2026, has developed a Linux variant targeting ESXi environments. The attackers deployed a custom ransomware called encrypt.out that uses ChaCha20 encryption and can selectively encrypt virtual machine files while keeping the hypervisor bootable. Between April 8 and May 21, 2026, Aurora operators used Cursor Agent, an AI tool running Claude Sonnet, to conduct hands-on exploitation across ten target organizations. The agent performed tasks including network scanning, domain enumeration, and NTLM relay attacks, with strict restrictions imposed by operators against DCSync attacks, account lockouts, and adding new computer objects to domains.

Researchers identified a second cluster of Aurora activity affecting eight victim organizations across Israel, Germany, Austria, Spain, the United States, and Argentina. This second group used different techniques including SQL Server exploitation and data exfiltration to self-hosted S3 storage. Aurora operates a data leak site and demands ransom through a Tor portal, with victims receiving access keys after their files are encrypted. The investigation provided indicators of compromise including multiple IP addresses, URLs, and file hashes to help organizations identify and defend against Aurora ransomware attacks.
